questions.prompt: Carol says that show business is ruthless. Which pair of words gives the meaning of that adjective?

options.text: cruel and pitiless
honest and fair
noisy and tiring
rich and admired

questions.explanation: "cruel and pitiless" is the meaning the book gives for ruthless: a ruthless world drops a singer the day her record sells less. "rich and admired" describes what people see from outside, not the hardness Carol is talking about. "honest and fair" would be the opposite of her sentence, and "noisy and tiring" describes a concert hall, not a way of treating people.

questions.prompt: The journalist asks Carol: "How much pocket money do you get?" Which of these four answers has the right shape for that question?

options.text: At twenty-one.
My mother, without any doubt.
Eighty pounds every month.
At the school I go to.

questions.explanation: "Eighty pounds every month." is the only answer with the right shape: How much asks for a sum, and this one gives a sum and says how often it comes. "At twenty-one." gives an age, which is what a When...? question waits for. "My mother, without any doubt." gives a person, and that answers a Who...? question. "At the school I go to." gives a place, and that answers a Where...? question. All three are good English; they simply belong to other questions.

questions.prompt: The newspapers write a great deal about Carol's looks. What are they writing about?

options.text: her nearest relatives at home
her physical appearance
her plans for the future
her ideas about her old school

questions.explanation: "her physical appearance" is right: in English somebody's looks are the way that person looks, which is why Carol answers that she is not skinny and does not mind. "her ideas about her old school" and "her plans for the future" belong to other questions of the interview, and "her nearest relatives at home" would be her family, the topic of the question about her mother.

questions.prompt: You are writing a question for next week's oral test, and it must ask a classmate what he thinks of Carol's answers. Which one does the job?

options.text: How you like her answers to the journalist?
How do you like her answers to the journalist?
How often do you read interviews in the newspaper?
How many questions did the journalist ask her in all?

questions.explanation: "How do you like her answers to the journalist?" does the job twice over: it uses the frame this lesson adds, How + do + subject + like, with the thing you ask about placed straight after the verb, and what it asks for is your classmate's own judgement. "How you like her answers to the journalist?" wants that same judgement but drops the auxiliary do, which an English question of this kind cannot do. "How often do you read interviews in the newspaper?" asks about a habit, and "How many questions did the journalist ask her in all?" asks for a figure that is already in the text: neither of them asks anybody what he thinks.

questions.prompt: Four teenagers say what they did with a whole month's pocket money. Which one has allowed herself an extravagance?

options.text: Rim put the whole sum aside for her school books next year.
Sarra paid the bus fare to school with all of it.
Ines spent nothing and made the whole class laugh all week.
Nour spent it all on one silk scarf she did not need.

questions.explanation: "Nour spent it all on one silk scarf she did not need." is the extravagance: the English word names something costly that you buy for the pleasure of it and could perfectly well live without, and a whole month's money on one scarf is exactly that. "Sarra paid the bus fare to school with all of it." and "Rim put the whole sum aside for her school books next year." both go on things she cannot do without, so neither of them is a treat. "Ines spent nothing and made the whole class laugh all week." is the trap for a French speaker: the French word that looks the same points at odd behaviour, while the English one always points at what was bought.
